data.title: EMERGING MARKETS-EM equities eye biggest weekly drop since 2020 on AI rout, rate concerns
data.description:
* EM equities suffer worst week since 2020

* EM debt suffers biggest outflow since 2020

* Hungary's wage deal offers support to consumption

By Tharuniyaa Lakshmi

Nov 20 (Reuters) - Emerging market stocks were on track for their biggest weekly drop since the COVID-19 pandemic selloff of 2020, as worries over a potential AI slowdown hammered tech-heavy Asian markets on Friday, while the prospects of higher US interest rates kept currencies under pressure.

Stocks in Taiwan plunged 6% to record their biggest weekly decline since 1990, while South Korea's Kospi fell more than 5% as investors unwound AI-linked bets across the globe despite a record-breaking debut for Anthropic and strong forecasts from chip giant Nvidia ( NVDA ).

Tech stocks across the globe have sold off sharply in recent weeks as worries about tighter US regulation on data centre development and chip exports as well as the abrupt exit of Jensen Huang as Nvidia's ( NVDA ) CEO fuelled concerns about the future of AI, especially after explosive growth in the technology boosted stock markets and economies this year.

MSCI's emerging market equities index fell 3%, on track to wipe out most of its year-to-date gains, in a sharp reversal from mid-June when it was up nearly 29%.

"The pillars of EM leadership are shifting. AI powered an exceptional 2026, but higher funding costs increasingly expose the ROIC-destructive economics of hyperscaler capex," Jefferies analysts said.

"A moderation in AI investment could trigger EM earnings downgrades, led by Korea and Taiwan, while India and China offer relative earnings resilience."

Indian stocks have been a rare bright spot, trading at nine-month highs, helped by a relative lack of exposure to AI companies and a sharp retreat in oil prices.

Equity markets in emerging Europe dropped too, with Poland's WIG20 down nearly 3% and Hungary's Budapest SE index falling 2.3%.

US RATE WORRIES

The MSCI EM currencies index dipped 0.1% and was set for its fourth consecutive weekly decline.

In South Africa, the rand hovered just below one-year lows against the dollar, on increasing bets on US interest rate hikes and the South African central bank's decision to keep interest rates unchanged. The currency steadied at 17.45 per dollar, having touched a one-year low of 17.56 earlier in the session.

Investor caution was also evident in debt markets, with Bank of America data showing EM debt funds recorded outflows of $7.5 billion in the latest week ending November 18, the largest withdrawal since April 2020.

In Hungary, meanwhile, the government said gross minimum wages would rise by 7.5% to 347,000 forints ($1,020.44) next year under an agreement reached late on Thursday with employers and trade unions, offering some support to domestic demand prospects.

The Hungarian forint weakened 0.3% against the euro, as investors awaited Moody's review of Hungary's sovereign rating later in the day.

The Polish zloty fell 0.4% amid fading hopes for a breakthrough in Ukraine. Polish authorities said they were investigating reports that at least two unidentified objects had fallen near the Ukrainian border after the military said the country's airspace may have been violated during Russian strikes on Ukraine.​‌

Investors were also keeping a close watch on developments in the Middle East.

Brent crude fell nearly 1% as robust crude exports from the Middle East eased supply concerns, overshadowing Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia's capital Riyadh and reports of tanker disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz.​‌

(Reporting by Tharuniyaa Lakshmi and Sruthi Shankar in Bengaluru, Editing by Louise Heavens)

data.title: FOREX-Dollar set for fourth weekly gain, supported by Fed tightening expectations, AI-driven haven bid
data.description:
* Dollar index near strongest since early April 2025

* Markets debating size, not likelihood, of December Fed hike

* Yen firms after Japanese core inflation hits 2.2%

(Updates throughout)

By Sophie Kiderlin

LONDON, Nov 20 (Reuters) - The dollar was steady on Friday and was on track to rise for the fourth straight week as expectations of further Federal Reserve tightening underpinned the US currency and jitters over the AI trade sent investors fleeing to safe-haven assets.

The dollar index was perched near the 103.9 level, around its strongest since early April 2025. The weeks-long rally accelerated on November 10, when hotter-than-expected US inflation data reinforced bets that the Federal Reserve would tighten policy and Fed Governor Christopher Waller said a 50-basis-point hike in December should be considered.

The dollar was also supported by a reduced appetite for risk, with a multitude of AI-related concerns weighing on global stocks. Anthropic's record market debut on Thursday did little to revive investor confidence.

MSCI's world index of stocks fell for a seventh straight session on Friday, the longest losing streak since 2023.

Chris Turner, global head of markets at ING, said that while there is only a weak case for another steep correction in equities, "there is no reason for the Fed to drop its hawkish rhetoric anytime soon."

He pointed to next week's US personal consumption expenditures (PCE) report, a key inflation gauge for the Fed, which Turner said will likely confirm that the Fed needs to act.

"For FX, that means a continued strong dollar and continued pressure on popular carry trades," he said.

In FX carry trades, investors borrow in low-yielding currencies, such as the Japanese yen and Swiss franc, to fund purchases of higher-yielding assets elsewhere, often in emerging markets.

Adding to the hawkish-leaning narrative, Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia President Anna Paulson said on Thursday the Fed will need to raise interest rates again because inflation is too high, while Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee said the evidence did not suggest inflation was heading back to 2% on its own.

"The debate now is not really about whether the Federal Reserve will raise rates in December, but how much it will raise rates by," Carol Kong, currency strategist at Commonwealth Bank of Australia, said.

"We still think 25 basis points is more likely," Kong added. "If they really want to quicken the pace of tightening, I think they will prefer to increase rates by 25 bps in consecutive meetings rather than deliver a bigger-than-usual hike."

Sterling languished near a one-year low against the dollar at $1.3105, and the euro struggled near its lowest level since April 2025 and last bought $1.0961.

YEN FIRMS ON INFLATION DATA

The yen firmed 0.6% against the dollar to 158.78 and is set to close the week with a small gain after three weeks of losses that had dragged the currency to near the key 160 level.

Japan's annual core inflation accelerated to 2.2% in October, staying above the central bank's 2% target for a second straight month and pointing to broadening price pressures that strengthen the case for a near-term rate hike by the Bank of Japan.

Analysts at Capital Economics argue the yen's recent weakness is unlikely to last. With long-term inflation expectations now around target, further increases in yields would be mostly in real terms, which, combined with their view that US yields will fall, should prove yen-positive, the analysts said.

ING's Turner also noted that a carry trade unwind should be a slight positive for the yen.

(Reporting by Sophie Kiderlin in London, Li Gu in Shanghai and Rae Wee in Singapore; Editing by Tom Hogue, Sharon Singleton and Andrew Heavens)

data.title: Canadian Two-Year Bond Yields Yet to Reflect Growing Disinflationary Pressures, BMO Says
data.description:
07:14 AM EST, 11/20/2026 (MT Newswires) -- Canadian two-year bond yields have yet to fully price in the mounting disinflationary pressures arising from the sharp drop in gasoline prices over the past month, according to BMO Capital Markets in a Thursday note.

Pump prices are set to fall by double digits in November, potentially pushing the annual headline consumer price index down to around 2.5%, well below the Bank of Canada's 3.4% fourth-quarter forecast, with a reading below 3% increasingly likely, wrote BMO in the note.

The divergence is particularly notable given the strong correlation between fuel prices, BoC rate expectations and two-year yields throughout 2026, said the bank.

Although this relationship appears to have broken down over the past month, the BoC has continued to highlight the risk of energy-driven inflation feeding through into broader prices.

With the energy shock now reversing, however, inflation risks may be shifting decisively to the downside, leaving two-year yields exposed to a repricing of the BoC's policy outlook, added BMO.
